meta.notes: Source of truth for the history layer. Frames are snapshots, not a continuous scrub: the archives support dated moments, not annual geometry. Dot anchors are [lon, lat] EPSG:4326 and the site projects them, same as trivia. A frame's verified flag describes the frame's own words; each event card carries its own, so an uncertain detail flags itself without casting doubt on the plate around it. ship:false frames appear on the scrubber and say they are still being inked.
honesty_footnotes: Past market footprints are drawn with today's utility shapes. Distribution boundaries move far less than market membership, but this is an approximation.

The county layer is a hand trace of the FTC's own plate, Map III, dated 1925 and drawn on modern county equivalents. It shows fields of operation, which is where a group ran utilities, not where it held stock. Uncertainty is kept rather than resolved: about one county in nine is visibly filled but its pattern cannot be read, and ambiguous counties name both candidates. The plate also cannot carry city-scale operators, because Map IV states in its own margin that separate cities and towns served are not shown and the same applies to Map III. Richmond, Norfolk, Baltimore and Washington are the known cases.

The line between the Eastern and Western grids is drawn from today's utility service boundaries, assigned by balancing authority. It settled roughly here by the mid-1970s. In three places, near Scottsbluff, Miles City and Rapid City, one utility's single shape spans the line, so the line there is the best this source can support rather than a surveyed border.

Market footprints are built by replaying 34 dated events from 1996 and requiring every utility's final state to match the live map. Where a market's founding roster survives in filings, which is PJM, a utility named nowhere follows the named zone nearest it. Where it does not, a utility not named in any event is drawn as a member from that market's founding. 185 utilities out of 1,956, 9.5 per cent, would land in a different market on the 1999 or 2005 plate under their second or third nearest zone. They are municipals and co-ops in Ohio, Indiana and Kentucky, in the gaps between the companies PJM absorbed between 2004 and 2012, and all of them agree by 2014.

The 1999 plate draws five markets because five were running. MISO's 1998 approval was conditional, its compliance order came in April 1999, and it did not operate until December 2001. SPP did not become an RTO until 2004. Neither is drawn rather than being approximated.
meta.dots_note: The 50 largest urban places of the 1900 Census, every one of which had central-station service, plus four small places that were firsts. Populations are read from the Census table, not transcribed. Generated by pipeline/11-build-timeline-dots.mjs.
meta.seam_note: Regions and both boundaries are built by pipeline/13-build-seam.mjs, which places twenty independently known cities in the right machine before it writes the file.
meta.membership_note: Built by pipeline/15-build-membership.mjs from membership-events.json, which carries the per-market rule and the reason for it. PJM is the regression test: ten founding zones plus eleven later joins reproduce its present-day zones with no residue.

frames.title: Islands of light
frames.body: In 1900 there was no grid. There were thousands of small ones. A power station lit the blocks around it and stopped. If you lived past the last wire, you had no electricity at all. Every glowing dot here is a city with its own station.
frames.note: The first stations ran on direct current. It could not travel far before the copper cost more than the electricity was worth, so a station lit the blocks around it and stopped. That one limit is why the map is dots instead of country.

legend.label: A city with its own power station

frames.title: The buyers start buying the buyers
frames.body:
The FTC drew this sheet to answer one question: who held what, county by county. A third of the country comes back blank. On 1,173 counties no principal power group operated at all, which is not the same as darkness. Municipal plants and companies too small for the FTC's list are simply not on the map.

What is on it got there by buying. A holding company bought operating companies. A bigger holding company bought the holding company. The men at the top never touched a wire, and by 1925 twenty groups had taken the parts of the country worth taking.
frames.note: This layer is a hand trace of FTC Map III, printed 1925, read to all 3,108 modern county equivalents. Counties the engraving cannot settle are marked unreadable or ambiguous rather than guessed, and the panel above says how the sheet was read. Modern county geometry is used to read a historical plate, so changed boundaries and separate towns remain limits of the trace.
frames.verify_notes: Map III county trace released with explicit exact, possible, ambiguous, unreadable, and unfilled states.

frames.title: A handful of men own the lights
frames.body:
Small companies got bought, then the buyers got bought. At the end of 1930 Samuel Insull's system operated in 32 states out of 48, two thirds of the country, and its rivals overlapped it everywhere. Sixteen systems together made about three quarters of the country's investor-owned power.

Seven years after the earlier sheet the blank third of the country is nearly gone: counties with no principal group fall from 1,173 to 195. It is also the last picture of the empires whole. Middle West Utilities went into receivership in April.
frames.note: This layer is a hand trace of FTC Map IV, printed 1932, read to all 3,108 modern county equivalents. It carries a circled numeral on many counties naming the operating company inside the group, which the earlier sheet does not. Counties the engraving cannot settle are marked unreadable or ambiguous rather than guessed, and the panel above says how the sheet was read and how wrong the reading might be. Modern county geometry is used to read a historical plate, so changed boundaries and separate towns remain limits of the trace.
frames.verify_notes: Map IV county trace released with explicit exact, possible, ambiguous, unreadable and unfilled states, an expanded machine-checked anchor set, and a published residual error estimate.

frames.title: One afternoon, two laws
frames.body: On a single day in August 1935 Roosevelt signed a law with two halves. One broke the holding companies apart. The other gave Washington authority over electricity that crosses a state line. That second half is the reason the map has a Texas-shaped hole in it: within weeks, two Texas companies opened their switches to Oklahoma and stayed inside the state.
frames.note: What makes a utility federal is not whether its own electrons cross a border. It is whether its system runs in step with one that does. Courts settled that on a commingling theory decades later, and by the 1960s Texas companies were being told they were federal with no wires crossing the line at all.

legend.label: Where one machine ends and the next begins

frames.title: The country becomes one machine
frames.body: In February 1967 federal engineers closed a handful of weak ties in Montana and Nebraska, and the Eastern and Western grids ran in step for the first time. Engineers had tried three times before and never held it past a couple of hours. This time it held for months.
frames.note: It did not hold well. The ties were opened again in July, closed again in December, and then pulled themselves apart 381 times over the next eight months. Texas was never in it.

legend.label: East and West, running in step
The East-West divide, closed this year

frames.title: The country settles for three
frames.body: The ties were opened for good and left that way. From here the country is three separate machines: the Eastern grid, the Western grid, and Texas. In 1975 the number of working connections between East and West was zero. There is nothing to draw across the seam, and that is the point.
frames.note: Two years later the first converter station opened at Stegall, Nebraska, and the two grids got one small door between them. Everything else you can see crossing the seam today was built after this plate.

frames.title: Somebody neutral runs the traffic
frames.body: A federal order in 1996 said a company owning transmission had to let competitors use it on the same terms. It did not say who should run the traffic, and it required nobody to hand the job over. Five regions did it anyway, for three different reasons. By the end of 1999 five referees were running and most of the country had none.
frames.note: Texas and California acted because their own regulators told them to. PJM, New England and New York acted because the 1996 order made tight power pools file one tariff for the whole pool. Order 2000 arrived in December 1999 and required a filing, not a decision.

frames.title: The markets get big
frames.body: PJM swallowed the Midwest one utility at a time. Chicago joined in 2004. Then seven American Electric Power companies and Dayton. Then Pittsburgh, then Virginia. MISO opened a five-minute market in 2005, and Southwest Power Pool became a market operator too. This is when the map stops being a few coastal experiments.
frames.note: Not everyone stayed. Kentucky's two big utilities left MISO in 2006 and have run outside any market since. Ohio's utilities switched from MISO to PJM in 2011 and 2012, moving a market boundary several hundred miles.

frames.title: The largest single day on the map
frames.body: At midnight between December 18 and 19, 2013, Entergy and its neighbours joined MISO. Twelve companies moved at once. A market that ran from Minnesota to Indiana suddenly reached the Gulf of Mexico, in a piece that does not touch the rest of it. Nothing else in the modern era moved this much ground on one day.
frames.note: The plate is dated 2014 by its market events, not by the reshuffle: Southwest Power Pool opened its own market and became a single balancing authority in March 2014. The Gulf expansion belongs to December 2013 and is captioned by its own date.

frames.label: Today
frames.title: Where it landed
frames.body: Seven market operators, and about a third of the country with none at all. The three machines are still three. The Eastern and Western grids touch at about seven converter stations that together move on the order of 1,300 megawatts, which is almost nothing against their size. Texas still runs its own grid, which is the 1935 decision still holding.
frames.note: This is the same picture as the Wholesale layer, drawn from the same data. Step back through the scrubber and watch it come apart.

dots.note: The 27th largest city in the country, and today it is Pittsburgh's North Side. Pittsburgh annexed it in 1907 over the objections of its own voters.
Boston, Cambridge, Somerville and Lynn are four separate cities on this map because they were four separate cities, each buying its own light.

pearl-street-1882.title: Pearl Street switches on
pearl-street-1882.body: Edison's station in lower Manhattan started up with about 85 customers and roughly 400 lamps. It served the First District, a quarter of a square mile between Wall Street and the East River. Low-voltage direct current could not reach much past that without costing more in copper than the electricity was worth.
pearl-street-1882.note: The first Edison station to sell electricity in the United States. Not the first anywhere: his Holborn Viaduct station in London ran earlier the same year. The picture of it in the 1902 Census report is an engraving, not a photograph.

appleton-1882.title: A water wheel in Wisconsin
appleton-1882.body: A water-driven Edison dynamo on the Fox River at Appleton lit a paper mill and a house. It could run about 250 lamps. Customers paid a flat monthly fee per lamp, because nobody had invented a meter for this yet.
appleton-1882.note: The first hydroelectric station running Edison's incandescent system for paying customers. The 1902 Census report captions it simply as the first Edison station, which is the loose version of the claim and the reason this card exists. Grand Rapids had been selling water-powered arc light since 1880.

great-barrington-1886.title: Alternating current works
great-barrington-1886.body: William Stanley lit about twenty shops and offices along Main Street in Great Barrington. He sent alternating current down the street at 500 volts and used transformers in the basements to bring it down to 100. That is the trick a grid runs on: push the voltage up to travel, bring it down to use.
great-barrington-1886.note: An experiment, not a utility. Stanley ran it out of an old rubber mill and shut it down by that summer. The town's electric company came two years later.

telluride-1891.title: Power sent over a mountain
telluride-1891.body: The Ames plant sent 3,000 volts of alternating current 2.6 miles through the San Juan Mountains to a 100-horsepower motor at the Gold King mine. It is the first time anyone generated, moved and then actually used AC to turn machinery.
telluride-1891.note: The day is disputed: June 19 is the date usually given, and one local account says June 21. Longer AC lines already existed, at Willamette Falls in Oregon. What was new here is the industrial motor at the far end.

niagara-buffalo-1896.title: Niagara reaches Buffalo
niagara-buffalo-1896.body: Just after midnight, 1,000 horsepower from a single generator at the falls travelled 26 miles at 11,000 volts to Buffalo, where it ran the city's street railway. After this, a power station no longer had to sit inside the city it served.
niagara-buffalo-1896.note: The first current went down the line at 8:57 that Sunday evening and reached Buffalo one minute after midnight, which met a contract deadline of on or before November 15.

pjm-pool-1927.title: The first power pool
pjm-pool-1927.body: Philadelphia Electric, Pennsylvania Power and Light, and Public Service of New Jersey tied their systems together and agreed to run their plants as one. It is the first large, fully integrated, high-voltage power pool in North America, and it has run continuously ever since. PJM still carries their initials.
pjm-pool-1927.note: Not the first pooling of any kind. Connecticut and Massachusetts utilities had shared power in 1922.

insull-collapse-1932.title: The biggest empire falls over
insull-collapse-1932.body: A federal judge in Chicago put Middle West Utilities into receivership, the largest receivership in American business history to that point. The company could not pay 10 million dollars of notes coming due on June 1. The court acted on a friendly petition filed over a claim of 8,000 dollars, and named Samuel Insull himself as one of three receivers.
insull-collapse-1932.note: Only the holding companies failed. The operating companies kept running and kept the lights on, so nothing went dark in those 32 states.

northeast-blackout-1965.title: The lights go out in the Northeast
northeast-blackout-1965.body: One relay at a station in Ontario tripped, and about 30 million people lost power across the Northeast. Connecting grids to each other had made a new kind of failure possible.

golden-spike-1967.title: East meets West
golden-spike-1967.body: Federal engineers closed a handful of weak ties in Montana and western Nebraska, and the Eastern and Western grids ran in step. Engineers had tried this three times before and failed: under six minutes in 1957, about two hours across nine tests in 1962, and two hours and five minutes across eleven tests in 1963. February 1967 was the first closure that held for months.
golden-spike-1967.verify_notes: The exact number and location of the ties is contested. One archival account says four were planned, two in each state; the Federal Power Commission's own 1970 survey counts three in early 1967. The card hedges to a handful on purpose.
golden-spike-1967.note: It did not hold cleanly. Oscillations built through the spring, and the utilities used a pre-agreed right to open the ties again in late July. They were closed again on December 3, and the link pulled itself apart 381 times over the following eight months. Texas was never part of this: ERCOT stayed separate throughout.

nerc-1968.title: The utilities write themselves rules
nerc-1968.body: After the blackout the industry set up a council to write reliability rules, with nine regional groups under it. Following the rules was voluntary. They did not become law for another forty years.
nerc-1968.note: The Federal Power Commission's 1970 survey dates this to 1969, against the council's own 1968.

purpa-1978.title: Somebody else is allowed to build a power plant
purpa-1978.body: PURPA told the federal commission to write rules making utilities both sell power to small independent generators and buy power from them. Before this, a utility could simply refuse.
purpa-1978.note: The price was capped at what the utility would have spent making the power itself. The 80 megawatt size limit applied only to small power producers, not to cogeneration.

epact-1992.title: Wholesale competition, on paper
epact-1992.body: The Energy Policy Act let independent generators sell power wholesale and let them ask for transmission access. Asking was still not the same as getting.

order-888-1996.title: Open the wires
order-888-1996.body: FERC ordered every utility that owns transmission to publish an open tariff, so a competitor could move power on the same terms as the owner. It set out principles for what an independent operator should look like. It did not require anyone to create one.

ercot-iso-1996.title: Texas goes first
ercot-iso-1996.body: Texas regulators designated ERCOT as an independent system operator, and it began acting as one that September. The label came years before the substance: ten separate utility control areas kept running the grid until they were merged into one on July 31, 2001.

caiso-1998.title: California opens a market
caiso-1998.body: California's independent operator and its power exchange started trading. Two years later the market failed badly enough to end retail choice in the state.
caiso-1998.note: California's regulators had ordered an operator into existence in December 1995, before Order 888 issued.

nyiso-1999.title: Five referees
nyiso-1999.body: New York's operator started, taking over from the pool formed after the 1965 blackout. That made five running: Texas, New England, PJM, California and New York. Most of the country had none, and about a third still does not.

order-2000-1999.title: FERC asks everyone to join one
order-2000-1999.body: Order 2000 told every transmission owner to file either a proposal for a regional operator or an explanation of why they had not. Filing was required. Joining was not. That is why a third of the map still has no market.

comed-2004.title: Chicago joins PJM
comed-2004.body: Commonwealth Edison moved into PJM, which put a piece of PJM about 300 miles west of the rest of it.

aep-dayton-2004.title: AEP and Dayton join PJM
aep-dayton-2004.body: Seven American Electric Power companies and Dayton Power and Light joined on the same day. The gap between Chicago and the east filled in, and PJM became the biggest market in the country.

dominion-2005.title: Virginia joins PJM
dominion-2005.body: Dominion brought PJM to the Atlantic south of Washington.

miso-market-2005.title: MISO starts trading
miso-market-2005.body: MISO opened a market where power is bought and sold every five minutes. Its reliability room had opened in December 2001, and it began billing for transmission on February 1, 2002.
miso-market-2005.note: February 2002 is the day the billing started, not the day MISO started running the grid.

spp-nebraska-2009.title: Nebraska joins SPP
spp-nebraska-2009.body: The only state where every utility is publicly owned put its power into a market run from Arkansas.

miso-south-2013.title: MISO reaches the Gulf
miso-south-2013.body: At the midnight boundary between December 18 and 19, Entergy's six operating companies and six neighbours joined MISO. MISO's own list names twelve. A market that ran from Minnesota to Indiana suddenly reached the Gulf of Mexico, in a piece that does not touch the rest of it.
miso-south-2013.note: MISO called it the largest grid integration ever done, and reported 65,280 miles of transmission and about 196,000 megawatts of generating capacity across 15 states and Manitoba afterwards. Entergy had run its own control area and belonged to no market before this.

integrated-system-2015.title: The federal dams join a market
integrated-system-2015.body: Western Area Power Administration's upper plains system, Basin Electric and Heartland moved into SPP, bringing the Missouri River dams with them.
integrated-system-2015.verify_notes: Often called the first time a federal power marketing agency operated inside an RTO. That superlative was left unresolved by the research and should not be stated flatly.

spp-west-2026.title: One referee, both grids
spp-west-2026.body: A group of western utilities switched on a second SPP market, this one on the Western grid. The same operator now runs markets on both sides of the seam, across 17 states.

caldwell-2026.title: A town changes grids
caldwell-2026.body: Caldwell, Texas had been an Eastern-grid island inside Texas. New lines were built and it joined ERCOT.

insull-empire-1930.title: Insull's system reaches 32 states
insull-empire-1930.body: Samuel Insull's Middle West Utilities controlled more than 85 utility companies. The FTC put its field of operation at 32 states and Canada at the end of 1930. More than five thousand communities were served, with a population above six and a half million.
insull-empire-1930.note: Every number on this plate carries its own year, because the empires grew fast. The same company said fifteen states in 1923 and twenty-nine in 1929.

ebasco-1930.title: And so does Electric Bond and Share
ebasco-1930.body: General Electric set up Electric Bond and Share in 1905, and by the 1930s it was the largest utility holding company in the country. It sat at the top of five subholding companies, which together sat above roughly 237 subsidiaries at the bottom.
ebasco-1930.note: Bond and Share's own system reached 32 states too, which the Supreme Court recorded in 1938: the electric operations of its subsidiaries were conducted in thirty-two states. Two rival empires arriving at the same count is the fact worth keeping. A 32-state reach was not what made either one unusual. The count only closes by including American Gas and Electric, which Bond and Share held through a minority stake, so it is a judgment about what reaching into a state means rather than a gap in the record.

concentration-1930.title: Sixteen systems, three quarters of the power
concentration-1930.body: The FTC counted sixteen holding-company systems and added up what they generated. In 1930 they made 75.8 percent of the electricity produced by investor-owned utilities. The same table gives 80.2 percent for 1929 and 76.4 percent for 1932. A reader who wants one number for how concentrated this industry was should use the year they mean.
concentration-1930.note: The FTC says under its own table that these percentages understate the case, and gives the example: the United Corporation controlled Consolidated Gas Electric Light and Power of Baltimore on a 2.8 percent minority interest in its voting stock. The individual empires still cannot be added up or ranked against each other. The percentages in the record sit on different denominators and several of them count the same kilowatt hours twice.

ftc-investigation-1928.title: Congress orders an investigation
ftc-investigation-1928.body: Senate Resolution 83 told the Federal Trade Commission to take the utility holding companies apart on paper. The hearings ran for years. The finished record fills 95 printed volumes.

public-utility-act-1935.title: Roosevelt signs the Public Utility Act
public-utility-act-1935.body: Roosevelt signed the Public Utility Act of 1935. Title I is the Public Utility Holding Company Act, which forced the pyramids apart. Title II rewrote the 1920 water power law and renamed it the Federal Power Act, which gave a federal commission authority over electricity sold across state lines. One signing, two titles, and both of them still shape the map.
public-utility-act-1935.note: Congress said plainly that it was acting on the Federal Trade Commission's reports. The law's own section 11(b)(2) is the part that cut the stacks down: a company could sit one layer above a holding company, but not two.

texas-opens-switches-1935.title: Two Texas companies open a switch
texas-opens-switches-1935.body: Weeks before the new law took effect, two Texas utilities cut their connections to Oklahoma. Staying inside one state kept them clear of the new federal commission. Others followed the same logic for decades, and it is why most of Texas runs on its own grid today.
texas-opens-switches-1935.note: Isolation was not settled in 1935. It was nearly lost during the war, and the real test of it came much later.

texas-interconnects.title: Texas wires itself together
texas-interconnects.body: Texas companies had begun tying their systems to each other as early as 1924. A north Texas group formed first. A south Texas group grew out of the war, when Houston Lighting and Power ran continuously connected to its neighbours to cover wartime shortages. A statewide system was organised informally in the early 1940s and put on formal footing in 1967.
texas-interconnects.note: The war filled Texas with plants that needed power: shipyards, refineries, steel, a magnesium works, aircraft factories. Manufacturing output roughly quadrupled between 1939 and 1944.
texas-interconnects.verify_notes: The load driver is sourced as the scale of the buildout, not as an electricity figure. Do not restate it as demand growth without a source.

puhca-breakup.title: The empires are broken up
puhca-breakup.body: The Securities and Exchange Commission made the holding companies simplify. Pieces of them became the utilities people know now. Texas Utilities came apart in 1945, Middle South in 1949, Florida Power and Light and Pacific Power in 1950.

wscc-1967.title: The West organises too
wscc-1967.body: Western utilities formed their own coordinating council the same year, covering the whole Western grid.

ac-ties-opened.title: The ties are opened for good
ac-ties-opened.body: The ties between East and West were opened for good. They were not dismantled, just left open. From here the country runs as three separate machines: the Eastern grid, the Western grid, and Texas. In 1975 the number of working connections between East and West was zero.

stegall-1977.title: A different kind of connection
stegall-1977.body: Two years later the first link between the two grids opened at Stegall, Nebraska. It converts alternating current to direct current and back, which lets power cross without the two sides having to run in step. It was rated 100 megawatts, and a co-op built it.
stegall-1977.note: A widely repeated claim gives this first to the Virginia Smith station of 1988. Its own engineering award never says first.

midnight-connection-1976.title: Somebody wires Texas to the east
midnight-connection-1976.body: A Texas utility briefly closed a switch to Oklahoma in the middle of the night. It connected the Texas grid to the rest of the country, and it started a fight about whether that put Texas under federal authority. The courts were still working through it in 1979.
midnight-connection-1976.note: This is the proof that the isolation was deliberate and understood, rather than an accident of geography.

iso-ne-1997.title: New England activates one
iso-ne-1997.body: ISO New England took over from the pool that six New England states had shared since 1971.

pjm-iso-1997.title: The old pool becomes a referee
pjm-iso-1997.body: FERC approved the Pennsylvania, New Jersey and Maryland pool's plan to restructure itself into an independent operator, and it began work on January 1, 1998. FERC approved a plan the members had filed. It did not order them to file it.
pjm-iso-1997.note: PJM became a regional transmission organisation in two steps after that, provisionally in July 2001 and fully in December 2002.

spp-rto-2004.title: Southwest Power Pool becomes an RTO
spp-rto-2004.body: A pool that had coordinated the middle of the country since the war became a regional transmission organisation.

duquesne-2005.title: Duquesne joins PJM
duquesne-2005.body: Pittsburgh's utility joined. It later tried to leave for MISO, got approval, and settled the matter instead in January 2009.

lge-ku-2006.title: Kentucky leaves
lge-ku-2006.body: Louisville Gas and Electric and Kentucky Utilities left MISO after four years, paying about 27 million dollars net to get out. They have run outside any market ever since.

atsi-2011.title: FirstEnergy switches markets
atsi-2011.body: Three Ohio utilities moved from MISO to PJM after seven years and eight months inside MISO. A market boundary that had held since 2003 moved several hundred miles west.

deok-2012.title: Duke's Ohio and Kentucky follow
deok-2012.body: Duke Energy Ohio and Duke Energy Kentucky made the same move a year later.
deok-2012.verify_notes: Duke's own filings also record December 31, 2011. Both dates describe the same cutover.

nerc-enforceable-2007.title: The voluntary rules become law
nerc-enforceable-2007.body: The reliability rules the industry wrote for itself in 1968 finally became enforceable. The 2005 Energy Policy Act set it up. FERC certified the council in 2006 and approved 83 standards in March 2007. They took effect that June.
nerc-enforceable-2007.verify_notes: Chain assembled from the cross-plate reconciliation rather than from a single sourced finding. Verify each of the four dates before this loses its draft flag.

spp-marketplace-2014.title: SPP opens a real market
spp-marketplace-2014.body: Southwest Power Pool launched its Integrated Marketplace and became a single balancing authority on the same day.

lubbock-2023.title: A city changes grids
lubbock-2023.body: Lubbock moved its wires from the Eastern grid into ERCOT, finishing in December 2023. Its customers could shop for power for the first time in March 2024. About 70 percent of the city's load moved first, in 2021.

dc-ties-today.title: Seven doors between two grids
dc-ties-today.body: The Eastern and Western grids are joined at about seven converter stations, which together move on the order of 1,300 megawatts. Set that against two grids serving hundreds of thousands of megawatts and the two halves of the country are barely connected at all.
dc-ties-today.note: Counts differ. One federal table puts it at six by classing one station differently, and an independent history also counts six. Adding up nameplate ratings is also not the same as how much can actually flow at once.

ercot-federal-reach.title: What being separate does and does not buy
ercot-federal-reach.body: ERCOT is the only one of the three grids that sits entirely inside one state, and it carries about 90 percent of Texas's electricity. El Paso, the Panhandle and part of East Texas are on the other two grids. Staying inside Texas keeps most federal rate and transmission rules off its utilities.
ercot-federal-reach.note: It does not put Texas outside federal law, which is the most repeated myth about the American grid. The federal reliability statute exempts only Alaska and Hawaii. ERCOT pays the reliability organisation's fee, gets audited by the regional entity, and federal law contemplates FERC ordering transmission service inside ERCOT.

pacific-intertie.title: The long line down the West
pacific-intertie.body: The Pacific direct current intertie runs from the Columbia River to Los Angeles. It moves surplus hydroelectricity south in the spring and helps the Northwest through winter.
pacific-intertie.verify_notes: Length, voltage and capacity were all corrected during research and the figures have grown over time with upgrades. Do not print a capacity without checking which year it belongs to.

puhca-1935.label: The 1935 Act, section 11(b)(2)
puhca-1935.citation: Public Utility Act of 1935, ch. 687, 49 Stat. 803, section 11(b)(2).
puhca-1935.quote: cease to be a holding company with respect to each of its subsidiary companies which itself has a subsidiary company which is a holding company
puhca-1935.gloss: In plain words: you may sit one layer above a holding company, but not two. The stack gets cut down.
puhca-1935.note: The quotation this project showed before was not in the law at all. The phrase "first registration period" appears nowhere in the Act.

purpa-1978.label: PURPA, 1978, section 210
purpa-1978.citation: Public Utility Regulatory Policies Act of 1978, 92 Stat. 3144, section 210(a).
purpa-1978.quote: the Commission shall prescribe, and from time to time thereafter revise, such rules as it determines necessary to encourage cogeneration and small power production which rules require electric utilities to offer to (1) sell electric energy to qualifying cogeneration facilities and qualifying small power production facilities and (2) purchase electric energy from such facilities
purpa-1978.gloss: In plain words: if somebody else makes power, the utility has to buy it, and sell to them too. Before this a utility could simply refuse.

order-888-1996.label: FERC Order 888, 1996
order-888-1996.citation: FERC Order No. 888, Docket Nos. RM95-8-000 and RM94-7-001, issued April 24, 1996.
order-888-1996.quote: issuing a Final Rule requiring all public utilities that own, control or operate facilities used for transmitting electric energy in interstate commerce to have on file open access non-discriminatory transmission tariffs that contain minimum terms and conditions of non-discriminatory service
order-888-1996.gloss: In plain words: you cannot own the only road and refuse to let competitors drive on it. The order set out what an independent operator should look like and required nobody to create one.

order-2000-1999.label: FERC Order 2000, 1999
order-2000-1999.citation: FERC Order No. 2000, Docket No. RM99-2-000, issued December 20, 1999.
order-2000-1999.quote: all public utilities... that own, operate or control interstate transmission facilities must file with the Commission by October 15, 2000, a proposal for an RTO... or, alternatively, a description of efforts to participate in an RTO, any existing obstacles to RTO participation, and any plans to work toward RTO participation
order-2000-1999.gloss: In plain words: join a regional operator, or write us a letter about why you have not. The filing was required. Joining never was.

census-1902-stations.title: Central Electric Light and Power Stations, 1902
census-1902-stations.citation: U.S. Bureau of the Census, Special Reports: Central Electric Light and Power Stations, 1902. Government Printing Office, 1905. Public domain.
census-1902-stations.note: The first national count found 3,620 stations: 2,805 owned by companies and 815 owned by towns. Three quarters of them were in places with fewer than 5,000 people. That is why this plate is drawn as dots. There was no network to draw, only stations and the blocks around them. The count leaves out plants a factory or hotel built for its own use, so the number of generators in the country was higher still.

ftc-72a-table12-generation-by-group.note: Company-by-company generation, ranked. This is the table to cite for any statement about how much of the country's electricity a named holding-company group actually produced. Table 11 on the preceding pages gives the 1924 distribution of control, and the surrounding text notes that large local corporations held about 30 percent.

puhca-section-11-49-stat-820-821.title: PUHCA section 11, the death sentence clause, 49 Stat. 820 to 821
puhca-section-11-49-stat-820-821.archive: govinfo (GPO), United States Statutes at Large
puhca-section-11-49-stat-820-821.rights: United States federal government publication, public domain
puhca-section-11-49-stat-820-821.note: Section 11(b)(1) with the single integrated system rule and the adjoining-states test is on the page numbered 820. Section 11(b)(2), the clause that cuts a holding company off from any subsidiary that is itself a holding company over another holding company, is on the page numbered 821. Use this page rather than the fabricated quotation.

ftc-annual-report-1938-volume-list.title: The FTC counts its own investigation, 1938

ftc-72a-chart-9-insull-group-1932.title: Chart IX: the whole Insull group on one sheet, January 1932

ftc-72a-chart-10-insull-chain-1930.title: Chart X: one chain through the pyramid, December 31, 1930
ftc-72a-chart-10-insull-chain-1930.note: Seven layers, drawn as one column. Insull Interests, not incorporated, holding 69.3 per cent of Corporation Securities Co. of Chicago, which with Insull Utility Investments held 28.1 per cent of the voting stock of Middle West Utilities. Middle West held 99 per cent of National Electric Power, which held 93 per cent of National Public Service, which held all of Seaboard Public Service, which held all of Florida Power Corp, which held all of West Florida Power Co. and its $100,200 of common stock. The chart is dated the last day of 1930, and the FTC notes it is drawn before the receivership.

EASTERN.name: The Eastern grid
EASTERN.body: Everything from the Atlantic to a line running down through Montana, the Dakotas, Nebraska and eastern New Mexico. It all turns in step, all the time, which is what makes it one machine rather than a region.
EASTERN.note: It is the largest of the three by a wide margin.

WESTERN.name: The Western grid
WESTERN.body: The other side of the line, out to the Pacific, plus parts of Canada and Mexico. Its machines turn in step with each other and not with the East.

ERCOT.name: The Texas grid
ERCOT.body: Most of Texas, and nothing else in the country. It runs alone on purpose, and the reason is the 1935 plate: staying inside one state kept it clear of the new federal commission.
ERCOT.note: El Paso is on the Western grid, Beaumont and Amarillo are on the Eastern one. Texas is not the same shape as the Texas grid.
